# Designing the drift sweep before building the rig

**Generated by `scripts/71_drift_sweep_design.py` — do not edit by hand.**

Procedure 78 sweeps an imposed drift time constant and measures how monitorable the array is at each speed. When that procedure was first written its numbers were guesses. This works out what they should be.

> **This is a design calculation, not a result.** It assumes drift is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, sensor noise is white, and the monitor's risk tracks the window-averaged signal. Real optics will not obey that exactly. The output is where to put the sampling points, not what the rig will show.

> **The comparison target is the fault-free figure, not C18's.** The rig's natural-drift arm injects no fault, so it is compared against the fault-free no-overlap correlations from `scripts/70` (**0.085** on T11, **0.435** on T5), not against C18's pooled 0.902 and 0.784, which are raised by the injected ramp.

## The ceiling this measurement runs into

A block is 300 s, giving 55 windows, 10 of them once decimated to zero overlap. The sample lag-1 correlation is heavily biased downward at 10 points: feed it a series whose true correlation is 0.999 and the median value it reports is **0.60**. **No signal, however slowly it drifts, makes one block read much above that.** Any target above it has no corresponding time constant, which is why the first version of this script produced NaN when asked which drift speed gives C18's 0.902.

The two middle columns differ because of the small-sample bias: the third column is what the drift really does, the second is what 10 windows can see of it. The rig reports the second, and so does every no-overlap number already in this project.

## Where cortex falls on it

- **T11** measures **0.085** fault-free [-0.122, 0.453] on 17 episodes of 10 windows. That corresponds to an imposed time constant of about **11 s**, but its confidence interval runs off the end of the curve, so the interval is open-ended and the point estimate should not be quoted alone.
- **T5** measures **0.435** fault-free [0.271, 0.540] on 15 episodes of 7 windows. That corresponds to an imposed time constant of about **42 s** (interval 21 s to 72 s).

**T11 and T5 both fall inside the range the rig can produce**, which is what had to be true for the sweep to be worth running. Note that this is a much weaker statement than the first version of this script made: the intervals are wide, and on T11 the interval runs off the end of the curve entirely.

## How many blocks per level

Spread of the estimated r across repeats, at a cortex-like setting (tau = 26 s):

| Blocks per level | SD of the r estimate | 95% half-width | Separates adjacent sweep levels? | Separates T11 from T5? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 0.1467 | 0.2875 | no | no |
| 10 | 0.1109 | 0.2174 | no | no |
| 20 | 0.0798 | 0.1564 | no | yes |
| 40 | 0.0534 | 0.1046 | no | yes |
| 80 | 0.0381 | 0.0747 | no | yes |

With 8 levels log-spaced across the informative band, neighbouring levels differ by about **0.109** in measured r. That, not the participant gap, is what the sweep has to resolve to trace a curve rather than a smear. Resolving it means a half-width below half that. **No tested count clears it.** Eighty blocks per level still leaves a half-width of 0.075 against a target of 0.054. The half-width falls as one over the square root of the block count (fitted constant 0.672, worst residual 0.0129), so reaching the target needs about **153 blocks per level** — 102 hours of recording for the sweep alone. **That is not a feasible experiment**, and it is the central thing this calculation found: Procedure 78 as drafted cannot be run.

## The way out: fewer levels

Spreading the same band over fewer levels makes each step bigger, and the cost of resolving a step falls as its square. That is the knob worth turning before anything else.

| Levels | Step in measured r | Blocks per level | Total blocks | Recording time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 0.297 | 21 | 84 | 7.0 h |
| 5 | 0.186 | 53 | 265 | 22.1 h |
| 6 | 0.183 | 54 | 324 | 27.0 h |
| 8 | 0.109 | 153 | 1224 | 102.0 h |
| 10 | 0.080 | 286 | 2860 | 238.3 h |

Taking 25 hours as the most recording that fits the schedule, **5 levels at 53 blocks each** is the finest sweep that can actually be run (22.1 h). Eight levels, as Procedure 78 was drafted, cannot.

## Does the answer depend on the drift-to-noise ratio?

The ratio is set to 1.0 as a stand-in; it is a property of the built rig and is not known yet. At tau = 26 s:

| Drift-to-noise ratio | What one block would measure |
|---|---|
| 0.3 | 0.302 |
| 1.0 | 0.345 |
| 3.0 | 0.277 |

Spread across the range tested is 0.068, comparable to or larger than the 0.109 gap the sweep has to resolve. The ratio therefore has to be measured on the built rig before the sweep results mean anything.

## What to put in Procedure 78

- **Sweep range:** log-spaced between **4 s** and **811 s**, which is where the measured curve still has slope. Outside it the curve is flat and a level buys nothing.
- **Number of levels and blocks per level:** **5 levels, 53 blocks each** (22.1 h of recording). The drafted 8 levels at 10 blocks would need about 153 blocks per level to resolve, which is not runnable.
- **Report on the no-overlap spacing** (30 s between kept windows), against the fault-free cortical figures, and quote the estimator's 0.60 ceiling alongside any value near it.
- **The cortex comparison is weak and must be reported as weak.** The fault-free figures rest on 17 and 15 episodes; the sweep can say which imposed speed the rig matches, not that cortex has been pinned to a time constant.
- **Match the block length to the participant being compared.** T11 episodes keep 10 windows and T5 keep 7; the bias depends on that length, so a rig block of a different duration is not comparable without redoing this calibration.

## What this cannot tell me

- Whether real optical drift is Ornstein-Uhlenbeck. It probably is not exactly, and the natural-drift arm (Procedure 77) is the measurement that answers that rather than assuming it.
- What the rig will actually produce. This chooses sampling points; it does not predict the outcome.
- Whether the fault-free cortical figures are themselves reliable. They rest on 17 and 15 episodes and carry wide intervals (`scripts/70`).
